name: risechain/pevm (parallel EVM on revm)
workload: Criterion (100 samples) wall time to execute one whole Ethereum block with state preloaded in memory: 85 real mainnet blocks from Frontier to Cancun, plus three mocked 1-Gigagas blocks (raw transfers, ERC20 transfers, Uniswap swaps); sequential revm versus pevm's Block-STM style parallel executor.
claimed_speedup: Benches README: Uniswap Swaps gigagas block 413.42 ms sequential vs 18.707 ms parallel (22.1x); ERC20 Transfers 246.43 vs 60.817 ms (4.05x); Raw Transfers 159.08 vs 56.425 ms (2.82x). Mainnet blocks: 'We are currently ~2.02 times faster than sequential execution on average', max speed-up x4.32 (block 7279999, 4.54 ms vs 1.05 ms), max slow-down x0.89. Top-level README repeats '2x faster than sequential execution on average for Ethereum blocks, and 22x faster ... for a Gigagas block of independent Uniswap swaps'. In the 85-row mainnet table (counted from page data), 63 blocks are more than 5% faster, 18 are within 5% of 1.0 and 4 are slower (0.89x to 0.93x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features global-alloc (mainnet bench) and JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF=thp:always,metadata_thp:always cargo bench --features global-alloc --bench gigagas; workspace Cargo.toml release profile codegen-units=1, lto=fat, panic=abort; global allocator rpmalloc on x86 and snmalloc on aarch64 for mainnet, jemalloc with THP for gigagas; concurrency level 8 on x86 / 12 on ARM; rustc version not pinned (no rust-toolchain file, edition 2024).
tradeoffs: Parallel executor that still delegates VM execution to revm (an inline parallel-aware EVM is only a TODO). Speedup depends on block parallelism; falls back to sequential execution when a block self-destructs then redeploys a contract, and the concurrency level is hard-coded (8 on x86, 12 on ARM) with the README noting it ideally needs auto-tuning. Needs cmake to build snmalloc. Repo warns it is a work in progress and not production ready.
caveats: Baseline is revm run sequentially inside pevm's own harness (force_sequential flag / execute_revm_sequential), not an independent geth or evmone run; no geth evm comparison exists. Chain state is preloaded into memory, which the authors say understates the parallel advantage versus disk-backed state. The 22x figure is a synthetic mocked gigagas block of independent Uniswap swaps with no dependencies (README says it does not represent real-world blocks); real mainnet blocks average about 2.0x with several blocks at 1.0x or slightly slower. The top-level README's 2x/22x numbers describe the legacy Block-STM design; the 'new' architecture (inline EVM, sparse trie, shreds) is listed under TODO. No rustc version is stated, so tier A rests on public bench code, the release profile in Cargo.toml and a named CPU. Parallel Go (Polygon, Sei) being slower than sequential Rust/C++ is asserted in prose with no numbers.

name: revmc (revm AOT/JIT compiler)
workload: Criterion execution time in microseconds of three contracts (Fibonacci, Counter, WETH Contract) run through the revm interpreter versus revmc-compiled native code; the same-named fixtures (fibonacci-calldata, counter, weth) exist in the repo's crates/revmc-cli benches.
claimed_speedup: README chart 'REVM Compiler Improvement vs. REVM Interpreter' (Execution Time, microseconds), image only: Fibonacci 19.00x, Counter 2.77x, WETH Contract 1.85x. Read from the chart image; no table or text numbers in the repo.
stars_or_usage: 289 stars; integrated into Reth per Paradigm's announcement (search snippet only)
tradeoffs: Experimental JIT and AOT EVM-to-native compiler built on LLVM (needs LLVM 22, Linux or macOS only, Windows unsupported). AOT-compiled bytecode needs the revmc-builtins runtime exported in the final binary. Compile cost is paid up front (the bench has compile/translate and compile/jit cases).
caveats: The only numbers are in a README bar-chart image (19.00x, 2.77x, 1.85x; asset https://github.com/paradigmxyz/revmc/assets/17802178/96adf64b-8513-469d-925d-4f8d902e4e0a, read by viewing the PNG); the chart states no CPU, compiler or flags, so first-party tier C. The repo's current criterion bench (crates/revmc-cli/benches/bench.rs) runs interpreter vs JIT on OSAKA-spec fixtures but commits no results (it uses a codspeed cfg), so the chart cannot be matched to a current run. No evmone comparison exists in the repo or chart even though evmone is a listed baseline. A web search snippet of the Paradigm launch post (blocked here, not opened) and of a BNB Chain blog also quote 1.85x to 19x, and the snippets mention up to 6.9x on compute-heavy workloads and only O(1-10%) gains on mainnet sync; neither page could be opened, so treat those as snippet only. The 19x Fibonacci case is a pure compute loop.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/paradigmxyz/revmc README (chart image) and crates/revmc-cli/benches/bench.rs

name: rsjsonnet (Rust jsonnet)
baseline: go-jsonnet (v0.22.0-rc1 per the doc; nix pin b5ef4cd9c4e24f2f14a68ef3bda0ca3079e11e78); also C++ jsonnet (d33798d4) and sjsonnet 0.6.2 in the same tables
workload: hyperfine -N -w4 -m20 wall time per run of the Jsonnet CLI on 27 programs: real-world kube-prometheus manifests and GraalVM CI, C++ jsonnet perf_tests and benchmarks, and go-jsonnet builtin benchmarks (std.base64, std.foldl, std.manifestJsonEx and others).
claimed_speedup: jrsonnet docs/benchmarks.adoc (third-party, run by the author of competing jrsonnet): Kube-prometheus manifests rsjsonnet 57.9 +/- 2.6 ms vs Go 1068.4 +/- 16.5 ms vs Scala native 204.6 +/- 2.3 ms (C++ omitted, takes hours); Realistic 1: 7.8 ms vs Go 3158.3 ms; Realistic 2: 163.4 vs Go 3160.3 ms; Graalvm CI: 68.5 vs Go 600.3 ms; Large string join: 12.4 vs Go 46.4 vs C++ 39.7 ms; Tail call: 1200.9 vs Go 2559.0 vs C++ 18460.1 ms. Derived from page data: rsjsonnet is faster than Go in all 26 shared rows (geomean about 4.8x, min 1.09x on 'Comparsion for array', max about 405x on Realistic 1) and faster than C++ in all 18 shared rows (geomean about 36x, min 1.97x); versus sjsonnet native it wins 19 of 27 rows (geomean about 1.4x) and loses 8 (for example Inheritance recursion 115.6 vs 46.7 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Built by nix (jrsonnet nix/rsjsonnet.nix: rustPlatform.buildRustPackage at commit 27be31532180c611383ceb2b7f03193ab1253487, repo release profile lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort; go-jsonnet via buildGoModule, C++ jsonnet via its Makefile 'jsonnet' target); every implementation wrapped with --max-stack 200000; timing by hyperfine -N -w4 -m20. Compiler versions come from the flake lock, not stated in the doc.
tradeoffs: Targets Jsonnet 0.22 with a CLI similar to the official one plus two library crates (rsjsonnet-lang, rsjsonnet-front); MSRV Rust 1.85. Memory use is not measured in the doc. Pre-built binaries for Linux and Windows.
caveats: The only numbers live in the jrsonnet repo, not in rsjsonnet's own repo or README (no own benchmarks found). The table author maintains jrsonnet, which is shown fastest: jrsonnet beats rsjsonnet in 24 of the 27 rows (derived), and rsjsonnet is labelled 'Rust (alternative)'. rsjsonnet is slower than sjsonnet (Scala native/GraalVM) in several rows and C++ jsonnet has no row on the two real-world cases (the doc says too slow, takes hours) and on several others. Rsjsonnet is only shown as one run of a wrapped CLI process, so startup is included. Tier A rests on public nix build files with pinned commits and a stated CPU; compiler versions are implicit in the flake lock. The go-jsonnet row is described as v0.22.0-rc1 while the nix file pins a 2026-03-23 commit.

name: Gambit Scheme
baseline: Guile 3.0.11 (guild compile -O3); Chez Scheme 10.3.0 also in the same suite (Gambit is slower than Chez on aggregate)
workload: ecraven/r7rs-benchmarks: wall-clock seconds of about 55 R7RS benchmark programs (Gabriel, Kernighan and Van Wyk, Larceny set: fib, tak, ctak, mbrot, nucleic, ray, array1, cat, etc.), Gambit gsc -exe executable versus Guile precompiled with guild compile -O3.
claimed_speedup: From all.csv (derived from page data): gambitc-v4.9.7 is faster than guile-3.0.11 on 45 of 53 benchmarks with numeric times for both under the same name, geomean about 1.95x. Examples: fib:40:5 3.46268 s vs 6.489886582 s; tak:40:20:11:1 1.968017 vs 3.113433651; mbrot:75:1000 4.223346 vs 22.496891153; nucleic:50 1.545574 vs 5.551796865; ctak:32:16:8:1 3.573319 vs 83.031008426; cat:50 2.095778 vs 15.986089402. Slower than Guile on string:500000:100 (3.197634 vs 0.204681098), pi:50:500:50:100 (0.76942 vs 0.107659156), gcbench:20:1 (8.414929 vs 1.512640708). Versus chez-10.3.0+r7rs the same method gives geomean about 0.79x (Gambit faster in 17 of 54).
compiler_and_flags: bench script: Gambit 'gsc -o <out> -exe <file>' with no extra flags (safe mode, no 'declare (not safe)'); Guile 'guild compile -O3' then run with GC_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=100000000; Chez '--optimize-level 2 --program'; versions in all.csv gambitc-v4.9.7, guile-3.0.11, chez-10.3.0+r7rs. Packages built by the runner (ArchLinux packaging per README).
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; widely used Scheme-to-C compiler (Gerbil Scheme runs on it)
tradeoffs: Compiles Scheme to C and a native executable (gsc -exe) with an interpreter and REPL (gsi). Safe mode is the benchmarked default; unsafe declarations would run faster. Dual-licensed; the repo root holds LICENSE-2.0.txt and LGPL.txt (version 2.1) and the README states no licence, so the SPDX expression is inferred from those files.
caveats: Independent community suite, but the repo README names no machine, CPU, OS or measurement date, so tier B not A. The 1.95x geomean is a derived figure over rows matched by exact benchmark name; floating-point rows named with '35.' versus '35.0' in different implementations were not paired. Gambit's own bench/ directory commits no comparison results, and the Gambit repo makes no benchmark claim. Chez Scheme beats Gambit on aggregate (geomean about 0.79 derived), and Gambit is much slower than Guile on a few string and bignum rows. Lua was not part of the suite, so no Lua comparison is recorded. Gambit has one COMPILEERROR row ('compiler') in all.csv, excluded from the geomean.

name: Bigloo Scheme
baseline: Guile 3.0.11 (guild compile -O3); Chez Scheme 10.3.0 also in the same suite (Bigloo is slower than Chez on aggregate)
workload: ecraven/r7rs-benchmarks: wall-clock seconds of R7RS benchmark programs, Bigloo '-O6 -call/cc -copt -O3' native executable versus Guile precompiled with guild compile -O3.
claimed_speedup: From all.csv (derived from page data): bigloo-4.6a is faster than guile-3.0.11 on 36 of 50 shared benchmarks, geomean about 1.62x. Examples: fib:40:5 2.564524032 s vs 6.489886582 s; tak:40:20:11:1 1.762351104 vs 3.113433651; mbrot:75:1000 15.49738496 vs 22.496891153; cat:50 1.918521088 vs 15.986089402; sum1:25 0.335073792 vs 5.443149564; string:500000:100 0.438892032 vs 0.204681098 (slower than Guile); graphs:7:3 20.211041024 vs 6.8123056 (slower). Versus chez-10.3.0+r7rs the same method gives geomean about 0.63x.
compiler_and_flags: bench script: bigloo '<file> -O6 -call/cc -copt -O3 -o <out>' (C backend); Guile 'guild compile -O3' with GC_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=100000000; Chez '--optimize-level 2 --program'; versions bigloo-4.6a, guile-3.0.11, chez-10.3.0+r7rs. C compiler and version not stated.
tradeoffs: Scheme to C (and JVM) compiler; per the repo LICENSE file the compiler and tools are GPL (version 2 or later) and the run-time system and libraries are under the GNU Library General Public License (version unspecified); bootstrapping the git version needs an existing Bigloo (configure downloads one if none is found). '-call/cc' build option used in the benchmark.
caveats: Independent community suite with no stated machine, CPU, OS or date, so tier B. Bigloo has failed or crashed rows in all.csv (ctak ULIMITKILLED, mbrotZ COMPILEERROR, pi CRASHED, compiler COMPILEERROR, slatex CRASHED, chudnovsky CRASHED, equal ULIMITKILLED) which are excluded from the derived geomean. Bigloo's repo has a bench/ directory (bague, earley, fft, maze, etc.) but no committed comparison with Guile or Chez was found. Chez beats Bigloo on aggregate (about 0.63x derived), and Bigloo loses to Guile on 14 of 50 shared rows, notably graphs and string. Lua not part of the suite. Bigloo 4.6a in the suite is not necessarily the repo head.

name: Loko Scheme
baseline: Guile 3.0.11 (guild compile -O3); Chez Scheme 10.3.0 also in the same suite (Loko is slower than Chez on aggregate)
workload: ecraven/r7rs-benchmarks: wall-clock seconds of R7RS benchmark programs, Loko ahead-of-time compiled static binary (loko -std=r7rs -ftarget=linux --compile) versus Guile precompiled with guild compile -O3.
claimed_speedup: From all.csv (derived from page data): loko-0.12.1 is faster than guile-3.0.11 on 48 of 51 shared benchmarks with numeric results, geomean about 1.62x. Examples: tak:40:20:11:1 1.6679999828338623 s vs 3.113433651 s; fib:40:5 3.927000045776367 vs 6.489886582; ctak:32:16:8:1 19.98699951171875 vs 83.031008426; mbrot:75:1000 6.51200008392334 vs 22.496891153; cat:50 3.4140000343322754 vs 15.986089402; paraffins:23:10 1.7589999437332153 vs 3.866057371. Slower: string:500000:100 5.241000175476074 vs 0.204681098; pi:50:500:50:100 156.49200439453125 vs 0.107659156. Versus chez-10.3.0+r7rs geomean about 0.65x (Loko faster in 22 of 52). Loko's README adds an own startup claim: REPL starts in 1.2 ms +/- 0.2 ms on an AMD 3950X per hyperfine (no baseline named) and 'does fairly well in the R7RS benchmarks'.
compiler_and_flags: bench script: 'loko -std=r7rs -ftarget=linux --compile <file> --output <out>'; Guile 'guild compile -O3' with GC_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=100000000; Chez '--optimize-level 2 --program'; versions loko-0.12.1, guile-3.0.11, chez-10.3.0+r7rs.
tradeoffs: Written purely in Scheme plus some assembler; AMD64 only on Linux, NetBSD or bare hardware; no FFI; fixed heap size (LOKO_HEAP); ahead-of-time compilation only (no compiler in eval); inexact numbers use IEEE single precision only (per README).
caveats: Independent community suite with no stated machine, CPU, OS or date, so tier B. Loko has INCORRECT results on three rows (sumfp, nucleic, sum1) and a crash on earley, all excluded from the geomean; its single-precision inexact numbers may flatter floating-point rows. Pathological on bignum arithmetic: pi:50:500:50:100 takes 156.5 s versus 0.108 s for Guile. Chez beats Loko on aggregate (about 0.65x derived). The loko 0.12.1 result in all.csv may not match the current head. Lua not part of the suite.

name: TypeScriptCompiler (ASDAlexander77, LLVM-based TypeScript AOT/JIT)
baseline: V8 (Node.js) running the same TypeScript/JavaScript; no named comparison found
workload: No speed benchmark found. The only measurements in the repo are peak working-set memory for a ray tracer (256x256 and 512x512) and an n-body simulation under the compiler's own three memory models (-mm=gc, -mm=rc, -mm=none), which compare the compiler with itself.
claimed_speedup: No speed numbers. README says the compiler produces native executables, WebAssembly or JIT runs 'no Node.js or JavaScript runtime required' and states no speedup against Node, V8 or Deno. Only memory figures in README and docs/memory-models.md: a ray tracer at 114 MB under -mm=none holds 4.1 MB with reference counting versus 5.8 MB with garbage collection.
tradeoffs: Compiles a TypeScript subset with its own semantics (strict null checks, a custom default library for JavaScript built-ins, no JS runtime) to LLVM/MLIR native executables, WebAssembly or JIT; garbage collection by default, with reference counting or no freeing selectable via -mm. Runs without Node.js, so Node APIs and npm packages are not available unless its default library provides them (not verified). Builds against LLVM/MLIR 22.1.8 (prebuilt MLIR releases exist).
caveats: Tier D: no numeric comparison against Node, V8, Deno or any named baseline found in README, docs/ (memory-models.md and others), tslang/ or scripts/ listings, or in a web search. The README header badge says the project is developed by Claude Code. Included at tier D only because the seed list names it and it has 776 stars; a speed claim vs Node would need an independent benchmark.
